extra.message: SQL injection. `Student.create()` builds the INSERT statement with Python `%` string interpolation: `q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name})`, then executes the already-formatted string via `cur.execute(q)` with no parameters (line 45). `name` is fully attacker-controlled: `sqli/views.py:57` passes `data['name']` straight from the unauthenticated `POST /students/` form body. A value such as `x'); DROP TABLE marks; --` or `x' || (SELECT pwd_hash FROM users WHERE is_admin) || '` breaks out of the quoted literal and injects arbitrary SQL, allowing data exfiltration (including admin password hashes) and destruction. All sibling DAO methods correctly use psycopg2 bound parameters (`%s` / `%(name)s` passed as the second argument), which is the fix here.

extra.message: Missing authorization on a privileged operation. The `evaluate` handler, routed at `POST /students/{student_id}/evaluate/{course_id}` (sqli/routes.py:21-23), writes a student grade via `Mark.create()` (line 151) without any authentication or authorization check — it carries no `@authorize(ensure_admin=True)` decorator and never calls `get_auth_user()`. The admin restriction exists only in the UI: `sqli/templates/course.jinja2:41` hides the evaluation form behind `{% if auth_user.is_admin %}`. Any unauthenticated remote user can POST directly to the URL and assign arbitrary grades (0-5) to any student in any course. The `authorize()` helper in sqli/utils/auth.py:12 is applied only to `logout`.

extra.message: Missing authentication/authorization on a state-changing endpoint. `courses` handles `POST /courses/` (sqli/routes.py:18) and inserts a new course from `data['title']` and `data['description']` with no identity or role check. The intended control is client-side only: `sqli/templates/courses.jinja2:25` renders the creation form only `{% if auth_user and auth_user.is_admin %}`, but the handler enforces nothing, so any anonymous request creates courses. Input is also never validated against `COURSE_SCHEMA` (sqli/schema/forms.py:16), unlike `evaluate`, so unbounded title/description values are accepted.

Anonymous users can create arbitrary student records; because `Student.create` interpolates the name into SQL (sqli/dao/student.py:42), this unauthenticated route is also the entry point for the SQL injection.

extra.message: Jinja2 is configured with `autoescape=False` for the entire application, so every template expression renders raw HTML unless it explicitly applies `| e`. Most templates do not: `sqli/templates/course.jinja2:22` renders `{{ review.review_text }}`, `course.jinja2:14-15` renders `{{ course.title }}` / `{{ course.description }}`, and `students.jinja2:16` renders `{{ name }}`. Combined with the unauthenticated write endpoints, an attacker stores `<script>` in a course review (`POST /courses/{id}/review`, sqli/views.py:129) or a student name and it executes for every visitor of the course/student listing — stored XSS leading to session theft (aggravated by the non-HttpOnly session cookie).

cwe: CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')

extra.message: Stored XSS sink. `{{ review.review_text }}` is emitted without the `| e` filter into the course page, and application-wide autoescaping is disabled (sqli/app.py:35). The value originates from unauthenticated, unvalidated user input: `sqli/views.py:121` reads `data.get('review_text')` from `POST /courses/{course_id}/review` and stores it verbatim via `Review.create` (sqli/views.py:129) without applying `REVIEW_SCHEMA`. Any HTML/JavaScript submitted as a review executes in the browser of every user viewing that course.

extra.message: CSRF protection is disabled. The middleware chain registers only `session_middleware` and `error_middleware`; `csrf_middleware` is commented out on line 27. The CSRF machinery exists but is inert — `sqli/utils/jinja2.py:8` still generates `_csrf_token` and templates embed it (e.g. sqli/templates/students.jinja2:36, courses.jinja2:40, review.jinja2:33, base.jinja2:29), yet no request path ever compares the submitted token to the session value (the check in sqli/middlewares.py:26-38 is never installed). Every POST route — login, student/course creation, review, evaluate, logout — is therefore forgeable cross-site.

cwe: CWE-352: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)

extra.message: The session cookie is created with `RedisStorage(app['redis'], httponly=False)`, explicitly turning off the HttpOnly flag, so client-side JavaScript can read the session identifier via `document.cookie`. `secure=True` is likewise not set, so the cookie is also transmitted over plaintext HTTP. Together with the stored XSS above, this makes full session hijacking (including of the `superadmin` account) trivial.

extra.message: Passwords are verified against an unsalted single-round MD5 digest: `return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()` (import at line 1). MD5 is fast and broken for password storage — stolen `users.pwd_hash` values are recoverable instantly by rainbow tables/GPU cracking, and identical passwords produce identical hashes across accounts. The stored fixtures confirm the scheme (`migrations/001-fixtures.sql:10-13` uses `md5('superadmin')`). A password KDF such as bcrypt/scrypt/argon2 with a per-user salt is required. The comparison is also non-constant-time.

extra.message: Active debug functionality. The aiohttp `Application` is constructed with a hardcoded `debug=True` with no environment/config gate, so debug behaviour is on in every deployment (the app is launched this way by run.py:13 and by the container command in docker-compose.yml:23). Debug mode enables verbose internal warnings and developer-oriented diagnostics; `run.py:11` compounds it with `logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG)`, which emits framework and query-level detail to logs. Debug must be driven by configuration and default to off.

cwe: CWE-489: Active Debug Code

extra.message:
The 5xx error template renders `
{{ error.__dict__ }}
`, dumping the raw attribute dictionary of the server-side exception object to the client. This handler is wired to every status from 500-599 by `error_middleware` (sqli/middlewares.py:68-78), and autoescaping is off, so internal state — exception messages, database driver errors including failing SQL fragments, file paths and object internals — is disclosed to unauthenticated attackers. This directly assists exploitation of the SQL injection by turning it into an error-based oracle.

extra.message: The login handler (`POST /`) performs an unlimited number of credential checks: it looks up `User.get_by_username` and calls `check_password` with no rate limiting, throttling, account lockout, CAPTCHA, or failed-attempt counter. There is no such control anywhere in the request path either — the only middlewares are `session_middleware` and `error_middleware` (sqli/app.py:25-29), and no reverse proxy/gateway config exists in the repo. Redis is already available (sqli/services/redis.py) but is used solely for session storage. Combined with fast MD5 hashing and known fixture usernames, credentials can be brute-forced at full request rate.

cwe: CWE-307: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts

extra.message: Insufficient logging of security-relevant events. A failed login only appends a UI string (`errors.append('Invalid username or password')`) and successful login only sets `session['user_id']` — neither produces an audit record, and the module-level `log` created at sqli/views.py:19 is never called anywhere in the file. No shared middleware supplies it: `session_middleware` and `error_middleware` (sqli/middlewares.py) log nothing security-related, and the only logging call in the codebase is in the disabled `csrf_middleware` (line 33). Authentication failures/successes, authorization denials raised by `authorize()` (sqli/utils/auth.py:18-20), and state changes such as grade creation and course/student creation are therefore untraceable, so credential-stuffing and abuse of the unauthenticated write endpoints cannot be detected or investigated.

cwe: CWE-778: Insufficient Logging

extra.message: The `student` handler (`GET /students/{id}`, sqli/routes.py:15) returns a named individual's full academic record — every mark, its value and timestamp per course (lines 71-79) — with no authentication or authorization whatsoever. The object id comes straight from `request.match_info['id']` and is used to read any student's data; no ownership, role or scope constraint is applied. The same applies to `GET /courses/{id}` (line 96), which additionally enumerates all students. Any anonymous visitor can walk sequential ids to harvest the entire student and grade database.

extra.message: Session fixation. On successful authentication the handler writes `session['user_id'] = user.id` into the pre-existing session without first invalidating it (`session.invalidate()`) or otherwise forcing a new session identifier. A session cookie is already established for anonymous visitors before login — `index` writes `session['last_visited']` on line 29 and `csrf_processor` writes `_csrf_token` (sqli/utils/jinja2.py:13) on every render — so an attacker who fixes a victim's session cookie value (easy here, since the cookie is not HttpOnly) retains a valid authenticated session after the victim logs in, inheriting their privileges.

extra.message: `POST /courses/{course_id}/review` (sqli/routes.py:28-30) stores content attributable to no one: the handler never calls `get_auth_user()` and carries no `@authorize()` decorator, so unauthenticated clients can persist arbitrary review text to any course. The text is also stored without applying `REVIEW_SCHEMA` (sqli/schema/forms.py:8) — only a truthiness check on line 122 — so length is unbounded, and no author identity is recorded with the row (migrations/000-init-schema.sql:38-43 has no author column). This is the injection vector for the stored XSS and enables unbounded anonymous content flooding.

extra.message: Hardcoded database credentials (`user: postgres`, `password: postgres`) are committed in the configuration file that the application loads by default (`default_config='./config/dev.yaml'`, sqli/app.py:18) and that is baked into the production image (`ADD ./config /app/config`, Dockerfile.app:20). The credentials are interpolated into the DSN at sqli/services/db.py:15-18. Because docker-compose.yml:8-9 also publishes Postgres on host port 5432, these default credentials are directly reachable. Secrets should come from the environment or a secret store, never from a checked-in file.

cwe: CWE-798: Use of Hard-coded Credentials

extra.message: The schema bootstrap seeds accounts with well-known hardcoded passwords, including an administrator: `('Super', NULL, 'Admin', 'superadmin', md5('superadmin'), TRUE)` plus `md5('password')` and `md5('spidey')` for regular users. These migrations run automatically on database initialisation (`COPY ./migrations/* /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/`, Dockerfile.db:4), so every deployment starts with a guessable admin credential and no forced password change.
